newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: LME aluminium to rise; copper, zinc seen easier.
newsitem.headline: LME aluminium to rise; copper, zinc seen easier.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) aluminium prices are seen extending their rise later on Friday while copper and zinc prices are tipped to drift lower, Far East base metal dealers said.
"I believe aluminium's rise is not at the end yet," a dealer said. "The funds are the big drivers in this market."
Another trader feels aluminium prices "will push through $1,720 (a tonne). It's looking quite positive."
Three-month aluminium was seen by one metal house at 0200 GMT at around $1,711/15 a tonne against a late quote on the LME on Thursday of $1,712/15.
"We are looking for challenges of resistance to (the) recent high at $1,717 as the market continues to target $1,745," brokers Rudolf Wolff said in their daily review.
LME copper and zinc prices, however, are seen slipping with the red metal likely to be hit by some profit-taking.
"Copper will be sideways to downwards today," a dealer said.

Broker Brandeis said copper prices will find it difficult to move up due to the buildup in stocks and in light of the shrinking backwardation. Prices also closed weakly and below the 10-day moving average of $2,321 a tonne.
"Thus renewed downside pressure is likely," Brandeis said.
"There may be some further profit-taking in copper. We may see a pullback," a dealer said.
Three-month copper was seen by one trading firm at 0200 GMT at $2,335/40 a tonne, little changed from the late quote on the LME of $2,336/40.
Dealers said they have again heard talk that China may buy copper if prices fall some more, but they remain sceptical.
"That's what they've been saying since February and the Chinese have not come back to the market yet," one said.
Zinc prices are still trying to settle down after the gyrations seen earlier this week when prices dived from a seven-year peak.
"I think zinc will come down a bit," a dealer said.
Another trader said zinc should range between the $1,440-$1,450 a tonne levels for the time being.
"After all that has happened, it should trade sideways," a dealer said.
Traders said the market is still focused on what will happen to Chinese short positions , but the prevailing belief is that the severity of their predicament has eased.
"The Chinese have rolled most of their positions forward, but this story isn't over yet," a trader said.
Three-month zinc was seen by the trade at 0200 GMT unchanged from the late quote in London of $1,465/75 a tonne.
-- Rene Pastor, Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
